analysis.one_liner: Charges imports and US factories that emit more carbon per ton than their industry average, starting with fuels, steel, cement, and chemicals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2023 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat without a vote or hearing until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a carbon charge on both imported and domestically produced industrial goods — oil, natural gas, coal, paper, petroleum products, chemicals, fertilizer, glass, cement, lime, steel, and aluminum. A facility pays only if its emissions per ton of output exceed its industry's average, and importers pay when their goods come from countries that emit more per unit of output than the US industry. The price starts at $55 per ton of excess carbon and rises each year. About 75% of the money collected would go to grants helping factories cut their emissions, with preference for communities that lost manufacturing jobs; 25% would go to State Department climate and clean energy programs abroad. Goods from the least developed countries would be exempt unless that country supplies 3% or more of global exports of the good, and countries with their own comparable carbon charges would get relief.
analysis.who_benefits: American factories that are cleaner than their industry's average gain a price advantage over both dirtier domestic competitors and carbon-heavy imports. Owners of eligible facilities can win grants to cut emissions, with preference for plants in communities that lost manufacturing jobs. The public broadly gains from lower emissions and improved local air quality, since grant awards favor facilities in areas with high pollution burdens.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cleaner US factories and manufacturing towns

how_it_helps.text: Domestic facilities pay only when their carbon intensity exceeds their industry average, so efficient US producers gain a cost advantage over dirty foreign competitors instead of paying a flat carbon tax.

75% of the revenue is appropriated to a competitive grant program to reduce carbon intensity at existing facilities and build best-in-class new ones, with preference for economically distressed communities that lost manufacturing jobs, facilities that would most improve local air quality, and communities with high cumulative pollution burdens.

Importers pay a charge when a good's carbon intensity exceeds a benchmark that ratchets down over time — starting at the full industry average in 2025 and falling 2.5 points a year through 2029, then 5 points a year — so the incentive to decarbonize grows annually.
25% of the revenue funds bilateral and multilateral climate and clean energy assistance through the State Department.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas extraction, coal mining, petroleum refining, and the dirtiest cement, steel, aluminum, chemical, fertilizer, and paper facilities would pay the charge directly and would likely pass some of it to consumers through higher fuel, energy, and materials prices. Importers of carbon-intensive goods would pay at the border, and importers of finished goods containing these materials would pay starting in 2027. Costs at the gas pump and in energy bills fall hardest on lower-income households, who spend a larger share of income on fuel and energy.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel and heavy industry, then consumers

drawbacks.text: Charges on oil, gas, coal, and energy-intensive goods would raise costs that producers typically pass to consumers, so household fuel and energy prices could rise — a burden that weighs most on lower-income families who spend a larger share of income on energy.

Most of the revenue (75%) flows back to industrial facility owners as grants, so while the program funds cleaner production, it directs public money to private companies; the bill does include a clawback if a grantee fails to complete its project or hold its promised emissions reductions for ten years.

For imports from countries without verifiable plant-level emissions data, the carbon intensity is estimated from that country's whole-economy emissions per dollar of GDP, a blunt proxy that could over- or under-charge specific goods and invite trade disputes with major trading partners.

The compliance machinery is complex: annual facility-level reporting of emissions, electricity sources, and production tonnage, plus a petition system for special classifications, adds reporting costs for covered manufacturers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is more defensible than a flat carbon tax: domestic producers are charged only for being dirtier than their own industry's average, exports get refunds so US plants are not penalized in foreign markets, and the least developed countries are exempt. The real cost is on consumers through fuel and goods prices, and the scheme's economy-wide intensity estimate for many imports is crude. On balance it would push heavy industry toward lower emissions while shielding efficient domestic producers — but the consumer price effects are real and regressive, and the bill never went anywhere, so none of this was tested in debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and nothing else ever happened to it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the Clean Competition Act in the Senate on December 6, 2023, with Sens. Schatz and Heinrich as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
Four Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
No further action was taken — no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, coal, refining, and carbon-intensive manufacturers avoided the charge they would have faced, and importers of carbon-heavy goods continued to enter the US without a carbon price. No grant funding for cleaner factories was created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel and heavy industry importers

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Chair Ron Wyden and the Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee vote or hearing; the bill sat in the committee from December 2023 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Senate Democrats; no Senate Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced beyond referral in the Finance Committee.

industries.note: Petroleum, natural gas, and coal extraction are covered industries, so producers would pay the charge on production that emits more per ton than the industry average, and could expect to pass some of that cost to consumers at the pump and on utility bills. Avoiding the charge was in the industry's direct financial interest, and the bill dying spared them that cost.

Refineries, asphalt and petroleum product makers, and petrochemical and fertilizer plants are all covered and would face charges on above-average emissions. Fuel and fertilizer costs feed directly into prices ordinary people pay for gasoline, food, and goods.

industries.industry: Steel, aluminum, cement, glass, and lime
industries.note: The bill charges these industries only for production dirtier than their industry average, so relatively clean US plants — such as electric-arc steelmakers — gain a price advantage against carbon-heavy imports, while the dirtiest domestic plants lose. Grants funded by the charge would subsidize their transition to lower emissions, and lower industrial emissions improve local air quality in nearby communities.
Pulp, paper, and paperboard mills are covered industries; clean facilities gain an edge over dirty imports while dirtier mills pay. The cost would flow modestly into packaged goods prices.

industries.industry: Importers of carbon-intensive goods and finished goods containing them
industries.note: Importers would pay border charges on covered primary goods and, starting in 2027, on finished goods whose components exceed thresholds. Some would respond by sourcing from cleaner suppliers, which is the bill's intent.

industries.industry: Clean technology and industrial equipment suppliers
industries.note: The grant program would channel 75% of the charge revenue into purchases of new emissions-reducing technology at covered facilities, creating demand for such equipment and services.
